newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stealth fighters set to leave for Gulf.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stealth fighters set to leave for Gulf.

text.p: Radar-evading F-117A stealth fighters were set to leave for the Gulf later on Thursday to take part in possible air strikes against Iraq, U.S. defence officials said.

The F-117s, used against targets at the start of the war in the Gulf in 1991, are being sent from Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico to join more than 200 other land- and sea-based U.S. warplanes in the region, they said.
"All we're being told is, they're going to leave today (Thursday)," Second Lieutenant John Tews, a spokesman for the 49th Fighter Wing at Holloman, told Reuters.
No specific time for the departure has been announced yet.

U.S. officials said privately on Wednesday that eight F-117s would fly to Kuwait on Iraq's southern border. The United States sought and received permission from Kuwait, which was liberated from occupying Iraqi troops by a U.S.-led coalition in 1991.

Other officials said U.S. B-52 bombers like those used in the cruise missile raids on southern Iraq last week had been moved from Guam to the Indian Ocean island of Diego Garcia after Britain granted permission for them to be based there for a month.
In Baghdad, Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz warned Kuwait against permitting U.S. warplanes to use its territory for any strikes against Iraq, saying the move was an act of war.
"We consider this conduct on the part of the Kuwaiti regime a flagrant aggression against Iraq and an act of war against the state of Iraq," he said in a statement.
The United States stepped up attack preparations after Iraq fired a Soviet-built SA-6 missile on Wednesday at two U.S. jet fighters patrolling the "no-fly" zone in northern Iraq.
U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said that Iraq's air defence crews had been "playing some kind of a game, and they will very soon learn that we are not playing games."
"The responses that we will make ... will be disproportionate with the provocations which are made against us," Perry said on Wednesday.
